member.name: T:Proxmark3.Em410x
member.summary: The EM410x format, the common 125 kHz access tag: a 40-bit id sent over and over as a 64-bit frame — a 9-bit all-ones header, ten rows of 4 id bits each followed by an even row parity, four column parities, and a stop bit of 0 — Manchester-coded by ASK at RF/64. Encodes an id into that frame (to clone it onto a T5577) and demodulates the frame out of raw ADC samples captured from the coil.

member.name: F:Proxmark3.Em410x.T55xxConfig

member.name: M:Proxmark3.Em410x.T55xxBlocks(System.UInt64)
member.summary: What to write to a T5577 to make it an EM410x tag with this id: the config word, then the frame split across data blocks 1 and 2.

member.name: M:Proxmark3.Em410x.Demodulate(System.Byte[])
member.summary: Best-effort demodulation of raw 125 kHz samples: centre the signal, find the half-bit length from the dominant short-run cluster, turn runs into half-bits, Manchester-decode, then locate a valid frame and return its 40-bit id. Null if none is found.

member.name: M:Proxmark3.Em410x.Runs(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte})
member.summary: The capture as runs of a constant level: each run's level and its length in samples. The samples are unsigned ADC bytes around a DC level, so they are centred on their mean and a simple sign gives the level.

member.name: M:Proxmark3.Em410x.HalfBitLength(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32})
member.summary: Samples per half-bit, from the dominant *short* run cluster: of the run lengths (3 samples or more) that occur often, the weighted mean of those near the shortest. Using the absolute shortest run made one noise glitch set the bit length wrong and nothing decoded. Null when no run is long enough to be signal.

member.summary: Each run as whole half-bits (run ≈ half → 1, run ≈ 2·half → 2). Robust to the ±1 jitter in run length; fixed-step sampling drifted into bit errors over a 64-bit frame.

member.name: T:Proxmark3.ProxmarkFrame
member.summary: The Proxmark3's wire framing as pure byte work, with no USB in it: the OLD 544-byte command and reply frames every firmware speaks, and the newer "NG" framing, used only to learn whether a firmware is a modern build. From the Proxmark3 source, include/pm3_cmd.h.

remarks.para: OLD: a fixed 544-byte frame — a 64-bit command, then three 64-bit args, then 512 data bytes, all little-endian, with no magic. A reply has the same shape. The app uses this framing for every operation: a 2016 Proxmark3 Easy speaks only OLD, and newer firmware (Iceman/RRG) still accepts it.

NG: a host→device command is an 8-byte preamble — magic 0x61334D50 ("PM3a", little-endian so the bytes read 50 4D 33 61), then a 16-bit field holding a 15-bit length with the top bit set to mean "NG", then the 16-bit command — followed by the data and a 2-byte postamble. Over USB the link is reliable, so the postamble carries the magic 0x3361 ("a3") in place of a real CRC and the device does not check it. A device→host response mirrors this with magic 0x62334D50 ("PM3b"); seeing that header back is the proof the firmware understands NG.

member.name: T:Proxmark3.ProxmarkLink
member.summary: One open CDC serial connection to the Proxmark: the device opened, its data interface claimed and configured, and the bulk reads and writes every command is made of — plus the drain → write → read dance each OLD command makes over it. member.name: M:Proxmark3.ProxmarkLink.Drain
member.summary: Reads and discards everything the device still has queued, until the bus is quiet. A command such as version makes the Proxmark send many packets; if they are left unread its USB TX buffer stays full and it stops servicing our writes, so the next command's write times out. Draining first keeps the link healthy.

member.name: T:Proxmark3.ProxmarkUsb
member.summary: A Proxmark3 attached over USB-OTG, driven through Android's USB-Host API. The Proxmark enumerates as a USB-CDC serial device; the app opens that serial interface once, keeps it open while the device is attached, and speaks the Proxmark's OLD command framing over it ().

remarks.para: This file is the client's core — the log, which device to use, the shared link and running an operation on it — plus the two link checks (probe, device info). The operations sit beside it: MIFARE Classic gen1a magic cards in ProxmarkUsb.Hf.cs; 125 kHz capture, EM410x reading and T5577 cloning in ProxmarkUsb.Lf.cs. Finding the device and tracking plug/unplug is ProxmarkUsb.Presence.cs. Underneath sit the open connection itself (ProxmarkLink.cs), the USB permission prompt (UsbPermission.cs) and the descriptor walking that finds a serial interface (UsbDescriptors.cs).
An instance is cheap and holds only how the caller wants to reach the device () and where its progress goes (); the connection itself is shared by all instances.

member.summary: HF (13.56 MHz): MIFARE Classic over the Proxmark's reader. A card's 14443-A identity always; its blocks only for a gen1a magic card, whose special command set reads and writes any block with no key — enough for a full dump, a block edit, or a new UID in block 0.

LF (125 kHz), which the phone's own radio cannot reach at all, so every byte here goes through the Proxmark. A read ACQUIREs raw ADC samples into the device's big buffer, downloads them, and demodulates EM410x () on the phone. A write clones an EM410x id onto a T5577 (the common rewritable LF card). Verified end-to-end on a 2016 Easy firmware: the acquire/download command ids are right, a real EM4100 decodes, and a T5577 clone reads back — provided the config block is written LAST.
Which USB device is the Proxmark, and whether one is plugged in right now. The host app's receiver for the USB attach and detach intents reports them here, and its UI follows .
